---
title: "Your first plate"
---

One continuous journey: a plate ID on an OMERO server becomes segmented,
measured single cells, then a local database, then a plot. Nothing here requires
reading the source code.

**You need:** a working install ([previous page](installation.qmd)) and the
OMERO ID of a fixed-cell plate you have permission to read.

**You get:** per-cell measurements attached to the plate in OMERO, the same data
in a local database, and one figure.

---

## 1. Check the plate's metadata

The pipeline reads the experimental layout — which well holds which cell line and
condition, and what each channel is — from an Excel file attached to the plate
object in OMERO. This is the single most common thing to get wrong, so look
before you run.

The sheet needs one row per well, with columns naming at least the cell line and
the condition, plus a channel sheet mapping channel names to indices. Channel
names matter: the pipeline recognises nuclear channels (`DAPI`, `Hoechst`),
a cytoplasm channel used for cell segmentation, and `EdU` if present.

::: {.callout-tip}
If the plate has been analysed before, the Excel file will already have been
converted to OMERO map-annotations and removed — that is expected, not a
problem.
:::

## 2. Analyse the plate

```bash
uv run omero-screen 1234
```

Replace `1234` with your plate ID. That is the whole command; everything else is
an override.

What happens, in order:

1. **Metadata parsing** — the layout is read and converted to map-annotations.
2. **Flatfield correction** — per-channel illumination masks are built from a
   random sample of 100 images and cached in a dedicated OMERO dataset, so later
   runs skip this step.
3. **Well loop** — for every non-empty well and every image in it: pixels are
   downloaded and flatfield-corrected, Cellpose segments nuclei and cells, border
   objects are filtered, cytoplasm is derived as cell minus nucleus, and
   `regionprops` extracts area, intensity statistics and centroids. Per-well CSVs
   are attached to OMERO as it goes, so a crash does not cost you the whole run.
4. **Cell-cycle analysis** — if an EdU channel is present, integrated DAPI
   intensity and EdU signal are normalised per cell line and each nucleus is
   assigned to G1, S, G2/M, sub-G1 or polyploid.
5. **Save** — plate-level CSVs and QC figures are attached to the plate;
   intermediate per-well files are deleted.

Expect tens of minutes for a full plate on a GPU, considerably longer on CPU.

### Useful variations

| You want | Add |
|---|---|
| Whole-well canvas segmentation instead of field-by-field | `--stitch` |
| Segmentation only, no cell-cycle or classification | `--segmentation` |
| A specific Cellpose model | `--model cp4:cpsam` |
| Live-cell lineages across timepoints | `--stitch --track` |
| A different environment file | `--env production` |

`--stitch` is worth understanding early. By default each field of view is
segmented independently, so a cell straddling two fields is cut in half by the
border filter on each side. Stitched mode assembles all fields of a well into one
canvas, runs Cellpose once on it, and excludes border objects only at the outer
edge.

## 3. Check it worked

Look at the plate in OMERO. You should see:

- CSV attachments on the plate object holding the final measurements,
- QC figures showing segmentation overlays,
- map-annotations carrying the parsed metadata,
- a mask image per field (or per well, in stitched mode).

Open one QC figure and confirm the outlines sit on cells. If the masks look
empty or wildly wrong, stop here — importing bad segmentation into the database
just moves the problem downstream.

For a closer look, the [napari widgets](../napari/) let you browse wells and
inspect individual cells interactively.

## 4. Import into CellView

The measurements are now in OMERO, but querying CSV attachments is painful.
CellView pulls them into a local DuckDB database.

```bash
uv run cellview import plate 1234
```

Then look at what arrived:

```bash
uv run cellview plate 1234      # summary, conditions, measurement counts
uv run cellview projects        # everything in the database
```

If the counts look implausible — a well with far fewer cells than its
neighbours — that is worth chasing before you plot.

## 5. Make a figure

Load the plate into a DataFrame and plot it.

```python
from cellview.api import cellview_load_data
from omero_screen_plots import count_plot, cellcycle_plot, save_fig

df, conditions = cellview_load_data(1234)

fig, ax = count_plot(
    df,
    norm_control="control",     # the condition everything is normalised to
    conditions=conditions,
)
save_fig(fig, "cell-counts")
```

`cellview_load_data` returns the measurements and the list of conditions found
in the plate. Every plot function takes that DataFrame and a `conditions` list,
so swapping `count_plot` for `cellcycle_plot`, `feature_plot` or
`classification_plot` needs no other change.

That is the loop: plate → analysis → database → figure.

## When it goes wrong

| Symptom | Usually means |
|---|---|
| Connection refused / authentication error | Credentials or `HOST` in your `.env` file; check with `omero-integration-test e2e_connection` |
| "No metadata found" | The plate has no Excel attachment and no map-annotations |
| Masks present but empty | A field with no stage position — a failed acquisition. Re-run that plate with `--delete` |
| Out of memory on a stitched timelapse | Add `--stream-stitch`, which stitches one timepoint at a time |
| Cell counts lower than expected near well edges | Known behaviour — border and foreground filtering removes cells more often than nuclei |
